newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville calmer on day nine of bloody standoff.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville calmer on day nine of bloody standoff.

text.p: France said on Friday it expected to evacuate all French nationals from Congo's embattled capital, Brazzaville, within two days and be in a position to pull out its armed forces.

The city itself emerged calmer from an eighth night under curfew, after an eighth successive day of clashes between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor, former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Witnesses and military officials in the capital of the former French colony where the two rivals both urged their forces to cease fire on Wednesday, described the sporadic overnight shooting and grenade blasts as less intense.
"The two parties have said they want a ceasefire and I think it is calmer today because of that," a top Congolese police commander at the international airport told Reuters.
Sassou Nguesso told a French newspaper an international peace force was the only hope of making any truce stick.

"For the ceasefire to be maintained, an international force must be deployed," he told Le Figaro daily in an interview, adding that a planned July 27 presidential election could not take place without international supervision.
Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, runner-up to Lissouba in the 1992 presidential election, has raised the idea of France forming part of a buffer force.
France has said that its troops in the Congo, over 1,250 foreign legionnaires and marine paratroops, would not intervene in the fighting and were on the spot to protect foreigners.
"We don't have a defence accord with Congo and I don't see why at this stage we should put ourselves in the middle as a buffer force," French army spokesman Henry Pelissier said on Thursday.
French troops have so far evacuated 3,420 foreign civilians, 1,410 of them French.

"We think there are less than 100 French nationals left in Brazzaville. Our main mission is to evacuate them if they want to go," Pelissier said on Friday. "We can start to think about ending our mission in the next 24 to 36 hours."
The fighting began after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to the July 27 election.
Kolelas's own Ninja militia, at the heart of clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 and early 1994 after a disputed parliamentary election, have stayed clear of the latest clashes.

Bodies lie unattended in city centre streets. Aid workers and military officials have not been able to reach all areas in order to compile a reliable death toll, which some sources say could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand.

Government troops and Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militiamen fought in and around the city centre on Thursday. Witnesses and military officials said the Cobras pushed Lissouba forces south west about one km along half of a four km front line.

Medical aid group Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Frontiers) has pulled all its workers out of Congo. They had been helping 5,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in a camp at Bilolo, 30 km (20 miles) from Brazzaville.
Sassou Nguesso, named president in 1979, bowed to pressure for multi-party politics in 1990 but was among candidates knocked out in the first round of the 1992 poll.
He returned to Congo in January after over a year in France and launched into an undeclared campaign for the presidency.
